title: Resolve Under the Bodhi Tree
hookLine: what a decision stands on, and a neighbor's picture of a face set firm
carry: adhitthana: decide once, then keep returning
tomorrow: what would you change if you'd seen where it all leads?

lines: THE GYM BAG BECOMES A DOORSTOP.
WHAT DOES A DECISION STAND ON?
cards: A new resolution feels like fireworks. A few weeks later the feeling is gone and the gym bag has become a doorstop. The decision didn't change; the feeling under it did.
So what is a decision supposed to stand on once the fireworks are over? The Buddhist answer has a name: adhitthana, resolve.

teach.h: SKIN AND BONES MAY DRY UP.
teach.b: The picture the tradition keeps returning to is the night of the awakening.

The story in the Jataka's introduction has the Bodhisatta sit down under the tree and resolve: let my skin, sinews and bones dry up, let my flesh and blood dry, I will not get up until I have awakened.

It sounds like a mood. But in one discourse the Buddha describes that resolve as something practiced: a steady refusal to shrink back from striving, not a burst of feeling. Resolve, in that sense, is a place to stand.
You decide once, clearly, and then you return to the decision instead of renegotiating it with every mood. This is a place where Buddhists have neighbors.
In Luke's Gospel, as his time draws near, the King James Version says of Jesus: "he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." Both pictures are a face turned one way and kept there.
The honest difference is what the resolve rests on. In Luke, Jesus prays to the Father, not my will, but yours.
In the Buddhist story, no one is asked for help under the tree; the resolve rests on the one who makes it. Different foundations, one shared posture.

how: Buddhists practice adhitthana by making a clear resolution, often at the start of a retreat, a vassa or a meditation session, and returning to it; the Bodhisatta's resolve under the tree is retold at Vesak.

o: a firm decision you keep coming back to
a strong feeling that you can do anything
a wish you make and then leave to fate

games.q: resolve, two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: I won't get up until awake

s: resolve is mostly a strong feeling
the Buddha describes it as practiced: not shrinking back from striving.
Luke's Gospel pictures Jesus' resolve as setting his face toward Jerusalem
"he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem."
the Buddhist and Christian pictures of resolve rest on the same thing
they share a posture; they differ on what the resolve rests on.

games.q: your friend decided to learn guitar. a few weeks in, the excitement is gone and she wants to quit. what does adhitthana suggest?
o: come back to the decision she made, not to how she feels today.
wait for the excitement to return before picking it up again.
make a bigger, louder resolution to get the fire back.
games.why: resolve is a decision made once and returned to. the feeling comes and goes; the place to stand stays.

practice: Sit up and turn your face toward one fixed point ahead of you, a door frame or a spot on the wall. Choose one small thing you're resolved to keep this year.
Each time your eyes or mind drift, bring them back to that point, the way you'd come back to the decision.

wordCard.voice: Adhitthana: resolve, the eighth perfection. A decision made once and returned to, not remade with every mood.

orig.note: Pali: resolve, determination; the eighth perfection.

carryVoice: Keep this one: adhitthana, decide once, then keep returning, the way the Bodhisatta stayed under the tree. Back tomorrow.
